Two tests added: (1) the 5th query (lead rows) throws after four successes -> sendTelegram not called, recordsProcessed 0, details 'digest failed'; (2) the 6th query (funnel) throws ER_BAD_FIELD_ERROR -> reported as SCHEMA BUG, proving the taxonomy does not degrade with query position. The mutation was confirmed APPLIED by grepping its anchor before the run (a mutation that silently fails to apply looks exactly like a passing test), and the source was restored byte-identical afterwards: md5 c1fce572c980e4b08e6d148db8dc0b7e on both the backup and the restored file, 18/18 green after restore.  Also verified: the demand line reuses the SHARED countActionableLeads rather than COUNT(*), so this cron cannot drift from dailyReport's lead definition â€” pinned by a 4-row fixture containing one callback-linked duplicate that must yield 3. operator-walkthrough-superseded-2026-08-.ref: WHAT THE OPERATOR SEES â€” a three-line overnight summary at the top of /admin (Today), above the decision inbox. It was written months ago, is referenced by a truth-guard test, and had NEVER been mounted. Nothing else on the page moves.  â˜… HOW IT WAS FOUND, AND WHY IT NEARLY WENT THE OTHER WAY. The reachability sweep listed MorningBrief.tsx among 8 unreachable page files and it was DELETED â€” then the suite went red with ENOENT, because server/adminTruth.test.ts opens that component's SOURCE FILE BY PATH and asserts on its text (F25e: live requires online === true, undefined is its own state). A file can be consumed three ways â€” imported, referenced by symbol, or read by path â€” and both an import graph and a symbol grep miss the third. It was restored, and the standing question recorded then ('unmounted yet pinned by a truth guard: wire it or retire it WITH its guard, never silently') is what this diff answers. Wired, not deleted.  ONE DEFINITION, TWO CONSUMERS. The brief needs the urgent-lead count, which lived inline inside the 'Urgent leads' SummaryCard JSX. Passing it to the brief would have meant re-typing the predicate â€” !isCallbackDuplicateLead && ACTIVE_LEAD_STATUSES.has(status) && urgencyScore >= 4 â€” and a re-typed predicate is exactly how the weekly digest nearly drifted from the daily report on the lead count, which is why countActionableLeads became a shared function instead of two SQL predicates. Extracted to one `urgentLeadCount` useMemo that BOTH the card and the brief read, so the header cannot disagree with the page it introduces. The memo sits ABOVE the isLoading early return; `lint:hooks` (audit-hook-after-return) passes, which is the check that would have caught it otherwise.  DEGRADES BY DESIGN: the component self-suppresses when there is no real signal (no yesterday data -> 'Quiet start'; no overnight activity -> line skipped entirely), so a dead morning renders less, never a fabricated all-clear.  â”€â”€â”€ ALSO IN THIS DIFF: the PII linter blind spot, closed and RED-GREEN PROVEN â”€â”€â”€ lint-pii's console rule used `[^)]*`, which cannot span a closing paren, so ANY PII interpolation following a call on the same line was invisible. The leak that shipped past it: console.log(`inv ${String(p.invoiceId).padEnd(7)} "${p.name}" ... ${p.phone}`) â€” a full name AND a full phone â€” while the weaker sibling statement on the next line, with no inner call, was caught. The rule was scoring the easy half. Widened `[^)]*` -> `[^;]*`: reaches across parens, still stops at a statement boundary so a match cannot run away into an unrelated statement.  THE WIDENING SURFACED 8, AND THEY WERE NOT ALL REAL â€” 5 raw leaks and 3 already-masked diagnostics (`***${String(caller).slice(-4)}`). A gate that flags correct code is a gate the next person learns to ignore, so the rule now sets `maskable: true`, joining the convention the log-field rules already use via MASKED_VALUE_SIGNAL. The 5 real ones were fixed by REMOVING redundancy rather than blanket-masking: two lines already carried the invoice id (and one the alg_estimates id), so the customer name was duplicate identification and was dropped; two phone prints were reduced to last-4.  ONE WAIVER, AND IT NEEDED A MECHANISM. `backfill-invoice-phone-from-customer.mjs:233` prints two customer names side by side under the heading 'given-name misses (surname exists â€” inspect before trusting)'. Masking that field does not protect anyone; it prints two rows of asterisks and decides nothing. There was no line-level waiver in this linter â€” only value allowlists â€” so one was added: `// pii-allow: <reason>`, with the reason REQUIRED so an empty marker silences nothing. Waived by SIGNATURE, never by filename.  RED-GREEN, BOTH DIRECTIONS: planting the exact original blind-spot shape (a `.padEnd()` call before the PII) INSIDE the very file that carries the waiver turns the audit red and prints the planted line â€” proving simultaneously that the widened rule catches the class it was widened for, and that the waiver is line-scoped rather than quietly file-scoped, which is the property a file exclusion would have destroyed. Probe removed; audit back to `clean (780 files scanned)`.  EVIDENCE: tsc --noEmit 0 errors; lint:hooks 'no hook-after-early-return patterns detected'; lint:pii clean (780 files); full serial suite green including adminTruth.test.ts, the guard that caught the deletion.  NOT CLAIMED: no browser screenshot of /admin with the brief mounted, and no live morning has rendered it â€” the composition and its degradation paths are asserted by the component's existing guard, not by a dawn run. Also NOT done in this diff and deliberately so: SMS_CONSENT_GATE was NOT armed. The operator authorised arming, but a read-only prod count taken first shows only 5 of 2,238 customer phone numbers carry an sms.opt_in row (0.2%), so arming would silence marketing SMS to 2,233 customers. That number is the whole reason the gate shipped in shadow, and it belongs in front of the decision rather than behind it. Prior entry (andon ramp) superseded per the rolling-manifest rule.  â”€â”€â”€ PRIOR DIFF, SUPERSEDED â”€â”€â”€ WHAT THE OPERATOR SEES â€” the admin's red / amber / green finally read at the same brightness, and money columns stop going ragged. This is a VISIBLE change and the only one in the diff; the customer site is untouched.  â˜… THE DEFECT, MEASURED FROM TAILWIND'S OWN TOKENS. Tailwind's palette is perceptually uniform WITHIN a hue and not ACROSS hues. At the shades this console actually uses â€” 1,881 occurrences across 52 distinct shades â€” its shipped OKLCH lightness reads: red-400 70.4%, emerald-400 76.5%, amber-400 82.8%; red-500 63.7%, emerald-500 69.6%, amber-500 76.9%. That is a 12.4-point lightness spread at ONE nominal step, running BACKWARDS: amber renders brightest, red dimmest. On a shop-floor andon board the colour meaning 'stop, money is at risk' was the quietest thing on the screen and 'caution' pulled the eye first. Equal step numbers were doing unequal work, and no component was wrong â€” the palette was.  THE FIX, AND WHY IT TOUCHES NO COMPONENT. Tailwind v4 compiles utilities to a var() lookup â€” verified in the shipped bundle: `.text-red-400{color:var(--color-red-400)}` â€” and custom properties inherit. So re-tinting the nine tokens on `.admin-shell` re-tints all 1,881 existing call sites at once, with zero component edits and zero sweep risk. Deleting the block restores stock Tailwind exactly; there is no migration to unwind. Scoped to the admin shell deliberately: the customer site keeps stock Tailwind, so no public page pixel moves.  CHROMA IS COMPUTED, NOT EYEBALLED. Each value sits inside its hue's maximum sRGB chroma at that tier's lightness, found by converting OKLCH -> Oklab -> linear sRGB and binary-searching the ceiling per hue. This matters because an out-of-gamut colour is silently clamped by the browser, and clamping shifts lightness â€” it would have reintroduced the exact drift being removed. The computation is also why the tiers sit at L 0.80 / 0.72 / 0.66 rather than higher: red's chroma ceiling COLLAPSES as lightness rises (0.191 at L70 down to 0.114 at L80), so equalising high would have bleached the one colour that must stay urgent. Red therefore keeps the most chroma at the text tier â€” severity now leads on saturation, which is a chosen signal, instead of on lightness, which was an accident.  TYPOGRAPHY: `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on admin `table/th/td`. Proportional digits make a currency column ragged and make a figure jitter as it re-renders. Applied wholesale to admin tables rather than per-component because a grid where only some columns align is worse than one where none do; 28 files already used it ad hoc, so this makes the rule uniform instead of partial.  EVIDENCE: client/src/__tests__/andon-ramp.test.ts, 8 tests, all green. It asserts the MECHANISM, not the literals â€” every tier is equal-lightness, tiers descend soft->text->fill, every colour is inside sRGB (same conversion re-implemented in the test so a bad edit cannot pass), red holds the most chroma at the text tier, and the tabular-nums rule exists. MUTATION-VERIFIED: raising amber-400 from L 0.72 to 0.78 turns exactly one test red and the message names the drift â€” 'tier 400 lightness values: 0.72, 0.78, 0.72'. Source restored and re-run green (8/8) before commit. BUNDLE-VERIFIED: the built CSS carries `.admin-shell{--color-red-400:oklch(72% .17 22.216);...}` for all nine tokens plus the tabular-nums rule â€” note the minifier writes `72%` rather than `0.72`, which is why a naive grep for the source spelling finds nothing and is not evidence of absence.  NOT CLAIMED: no browser screenshot and no measured contrast audit against the admin's actual backgrounds. The equal-lightness and in-gamut claims are computed and pinned; how the new tints look against every surface in the console is exactly the kind of thing only the operator's eye settles, so this is the one item worth a glance on the phone. If any signal now reads too hot or too flat, the fix is three numbers in one block. WHAT THE OPERATOR SEES â€” one MORE line in Monday's Telegram digest, and one admin API that was never reachable is gone. THE FINDING: `weeklyReport.generate` was registered in the tRPC tree (routers.ts:153) and had ZERO callers â€” `grep -rn weeklyReport client/` returns nothing, no cron references it, and the only other hits were the router's own file plus two test fixtures listing its name. `notifyWeeklyReport` in email-notify.ts was identically dead: the sole reference was auto-invoice.test.ts asserting `typeof === 'function'` â€” a test that proved the export existed and nothing more. The tempting read is 'nobody clicked it, nobody wants it'. render-spend-trajectory-superseded-1630-.ref: THIS DIFF ADDS A SECOND TRANSPORT FOR AN EXISTING PAID CALL, and the spend trajectory is FLAT per clip with one real risk that this diff closes. BASELINE. `generateReelClipVideo` already made a paid Higgsfield DoP generation per beat via the CLI. The new API lane calls the SAME vendor, the SAME model family (DoP), on the SAME account and the SAME credit pool, for the SAME one clip. It is not an additional generation and not a new spend source; it is a different way to place the call that was already being placed. It is also INERT unless both HIGGSFIELD_API_KEY_ID and HIGGSFIELD_API_KEY_SECRET are set, and no environment sets them today, so merging moves prod spend by zero. THE RISK THIS GATE CAUGHT, AND I HAD SHIPPED IT. My first version wrapped the API call in a blanket try/catch that fell back to the CLI lane on ANY error. DoP has no resumable handle, so a POST-SUBMIT failure -- a poll timeout, a `failed` terminal status, a completed-but-URL-less response -- means Higgsfield may already bill for that generation. Falling back then generates the same clip a SECOND time and pays twice for one beat. That is not a theoretical concern: 're-submitting is what doubled the paid spend on every timeout' is this exact vendor's recorded history, and it is precisely why the CLI path KILLS its child process on timeout rather than abandoning it. My blanket catch reintroduced the bug with a friendlier face. THE FIX. Post-submit failures now throw `HiggsfieldApiSubmittedError`, which carries the `request_id` and a `spendMayHaveOccurred` marker, and `generateReelClipVideo` RE-THROWS it instead of falling back -- one clip fails, one clip is billed, and reelPipeline's existing per-beat retry accounting owns what happens next. Pre-submit failures (bad key, DNS, connect timeout, a non-2xx submit, a submit with no request_id) spent nothing and DO still fall back, costing only latency. So the worst case is unchanged from today (one paid generation per beat) and the previously-possible two-generations-per-beat case is now unreachable. TEST EVIDENCE. server/higgsfieldApiClient.test.ts, 21 tests. Six are spend safety specifically, and they assert the error TYPE rather than a message, because the type is what the caller branches on: post-submit timeout, post-submit `failed`, and completed-without-URL all assert toBeInstanceOf(HiggsfieldApiSubmittedError) and that requestId is carried; non-2xx submit and no-request_id assert NOT that type, so the safe fallback stays safe. MUTATION-CHECKED: reverting the post-submit throws to plain Errors fails exactly 3 of the 21. The timeout tests use fake timers, which also pins the 60s floor (an opts.timeoutMs of 1 must still take the full floor). NOT VERIFIED AGAINST A LIVE ACCOUNT, so no spend was measured empirically: this was built from docs.higgsfield.ai and the official Node SDK and tested against a mocked fetch. `probeHiggsfieldApiCredentials()` is the free first step (status lookup on an impossible id -- 404 key works, 401/403 key rejected, anything else UNKNOWN) and spends nothing. server 410 files passed / 1 skipped (411), 4,619+ passed, exit 0; client 56 files / 1,019 passed; typecheck, lint:source, lint:pii, lint:brand-voice, lint:hooks, lint:sql, env:validate, validate:routes, migrations:check exit 0.

REVIEW ROUND 2 — four findings, all verified as real, all fixed. Two of them were holes in the very honesty model this panel is built around.

P1 · THE WRITER'S LATCHED disabled FLAG WAS NOT PART OF READINESS. llmLedger sets a module-level disabled=true on its FIRST insert failure and drops every later call until the process restarts. My readiness predicate read only the env var, so after one transient write error the reader would have reported a healthy ledger and the panel would have presented a FROZEN window as current usage - a confident number over a dead writer. Now ledgerRecordingState() returns on | off | stopped_after_error and the panel names the third case explicitly ("stopped after a write failure ... treat it as a snapshot, not as current usage").

P2 · RECORDING BEING OFF WAS HIDING REAL HISTORY. The first draft returned early when the gate was off, so flipping the flag off ALSO hid every row already written - taking the operator's data away at exactly the moment they would look for it. Writer state and read state are now two independent fields (recording / read); the read always runs, and the writer's state is reported BESIDE the data rather than instead of it.

The lane query caps at 100 (lane, provider) groups and I summed THAT for the headline calls/failures/tokens, so any window with more groups under-reported while the panel still offered to "show all lanes". 1. A REAL TIMEZONE BUG, caught only by compiling the SQL. The first draft bounded the window with gte(calledAt, new Date(Date.now() - days)). Drizzle serialises a Date bound to a TIMESTAMP column into a bare datetime STRING - measured exactly, params were ["2026-09-09 00:00:00.000", 100] - and MySQL/TiDB interprets a bare literal in the SESSION time zone. This is precisely what apps/nickstire/AGENTS.md forbids ("compute ages and day-buckets in SQL, not in JS") - a rule I wrote into my own research report and then broke. NEITHER NUMBER IS PROMOTED OR BLENDED. No combined score, no tie-breaker. Both raw readings survive on every verdict, and 'insufficient' names WHICH half is missing - an unreadable comparison that does not say which side is unreadable reads as 'fine'.
